metadata.title: ICT-related behavioral factors mediate the relationship between adolescents’ ICT interest and their ICT self-efficacy: Evidence from 30 countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 student background questionnaire and the optional ICT Familiarity Questionnaire administered in a computer-based mode to 15-year-olds across 30 OECD countries. The authors state that PISA sampling weights were used so that each participating student represents a larger number of students in the target PISA population, and they incorporate these weights in the statistical analysis to obtain population-level parameters. No replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported, so uncertainty quantification is described via bootstrapping for mediation effects rather than replicate-based variance estimation. The analytic sample is restricted to OECD countries that completed the ICT questionnaire, and the mediation models are estimated separately per country using multilevel mediation to account for clustering of students within schools.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2015 data and restricts to OECD countries that completed the optional ICT Familiarity Questionnaire. The resulting dataset includes 15-year-old students from 30 OECD countries (as listed in Table 1) with valid responses for the ICT interest (INTICT), ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT), four ICT behavioral mediators (USESCH, HOMESCH, ENTUSE, SOIAICT), and the control variables (gender and ESCS). Missing values across all variables are imputed using the EM algorithm in SPSS 20, producing a single imputed value per missing point, after which the multilevel mediation models are estimated with students nested in schools.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) ICT Familiarity Questionnaire — ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel random intercept/slope model per country: direct total effect of ICT interest on COMPICT (B range 0.4377 to 0.5703; Beta range 0.4385 to 0.6335; all 30 countries significant; 95% bias-corrected bootstrap CIs reported; BootSE provided in Table 4).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity Questionnaire the study leveraged ICT interest, student gender, and ESCS socioeconomic status to model ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT), finding that ICT interest had a consistently positive total association with ICT self-efficacy across all 30 OECD countries (B ≈ 0.4377–0.5703; Beta ≈ 0.4385–0.6335). This indicates that strengthening students’ ICT interest may be a practical lever for improving perceived ICT competence, though the mediation framework is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) ICT Familiarity Questionnaire — ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel mediation direct effects per country (Table 6): ICT interest → COMPICT direct effect B range 0.2750 to 0.3936; Beta range 0.2857 to 0.4173; all direct effects significant with 95% bias-corrected bootstrap CIs; BootSE reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity Questionnaire the study leveraged ICT interest, student gender, and ESCS socioeconomic status to estimate the direct (non-mediated) relationship between ICT interest and ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT), finding that the direct effect remained positive and significant in every country (B ≈ 0.2750–0.3936; Beta ≈ 0.2857–0.4173). This indicates that ICT interest is not only linked to self-efficacy through behavioral ICT use, but also has an additional direct association that can inform interventions targeting motivational beliefs.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) ICT Familiarity Questionnaire — ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT)
main_findings.target_variable: ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT) indirect effects via ICT behavioral mediators
main_findings.performance_metrics: Parallel multiple mediator model per country (Table 7): indirect effects a*b via ENTUSE and SOIAICT significant in all 30 OECD countries; HOMESCH and USESCH mostly non-significant. Proportion mediated (total indirect / total effect) ranges 19.25% to 40.15% across countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ICT Familiarity Questionnaire the study leveraged ICT interest and four ICT behavioral mediators (ICT use at school, ICT use for schoolwork, ICT use for leisure, and ICT in social interaction) to explain ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT), finding that mediation exists and is substantial (proportion mediated ≈ 19.25%–40.15%), with leisure and social-interaction ICT use (ENTUSE, SOIAICT) acting as significant mediators across all countries. This indicates that ICT self-efficacy interventions should prioritize creating opportunities for students to use ICT in personally meaningful leisure and social contexts, not only in school-based or schoolwork settings.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) using the optional ICT Familiarity Questionnaire, restricted to 30 OECD countries that completed the ICT module (total N=201,652 students in 7,708 schools). The dependent construct is ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT), derived from five Likert items and scaled with IRT; the key predictor is ICT interest (INTICT), derived from six ICT-enjoyment items, also IRT-scaled. Missing data across all variables are imputed using an EM algorithm in SPSS 20, producing single imputed values. Using multilevel mediation (students nested in schools; models run separately per country), ICT interest shows a positive total association with ICT self-efficacy in all countries (B≈0.4377–0.5703; Beta≈0.4385–0.6335). Mediation is substantial (proportion mediated ≈19.25%–40.15%), with ENTUSE and SOIAICT significant mediators across all countries, while USESCH and HOMESCH are mostly non-significant. Because the design is correlational and mediation is not causal identification, policy should interpret effects as associations rather than guaranteed causal impacts.
